retrieved_documents.title: Administrative Divisions of Afghanistan: Provinces and Districts
retrieved_documents.text: Afghanistan's administrative structure consists of 34 provinces (wilayat), which form the first-level administrative division of the country, and 401 districts (woleswali), which form the second-level division beneath the provinces. Provincial administrative boundaries are delineated by the Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), which is recognized as the country's authoritative source for administrative boundary delimitation. The AGCHO boundary dataset is distributed internationally through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) as part of the Common Operational Datasets (COD) used by the humanitarian community.
retrieved_documents.source: Common Operational Dataset - Administrative Boundaries (COD-AB), Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), distributed via UN OCHA / Humanitarian Data Exchange

retrieved_documents.title: Administrative Divisions of Afghanistan: Provinces and Districts
retrieved_documents.text: The AGCHO boundary dataset is distributed internationally through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) as part of the Common Operational Datasets (COD) used by the humanitarian community. The current 34-province, 401-district structure was established in the boundary dataset released on 22 October 2019 and was most recently reviewed for accuracy in July 2024, with reviewers determining that no update to the boundaries was required at that time. Each province is subdivided into a number of districts, ranging from as few as 6 districts (Nimroz) to as many as 28 districts (Badakhshan) in the AGCHO dataset. Provinces are governed by a provincial governor, and districts are the primary unit for local public-service delivery, including health, education and security administration.
retrieved_documents.source: Common Operational Dataset - Administrative Boundaries (COD-AB), Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), distributed via UN OCHA / Humanitarian Data Exchange

retrieved_documents.title: Band-e Amir National Park
retrieved_documents.text: In 2009, Afghanistan designated part of the Hindu Kush mountains, known as Band-e Amir, as the country's first national park. Located in Bamyan Province, the park contains six deep-blue lakes separated by natural mineral dams: Band-e Gholaman, Band-e Qambar, Band-e Haibat, Band-e Panir, Band-e Pudina, and Band-e Zulfiqar. The park is one of Afghanistan's most visited natural attractions.

evidence.query: Which Afghan government ministry is responsible for telecommunications and IT policy?

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) is the government body responsible for telecommunications policy, internet-sector regulation and information-technology development in Afghanistan. Its published areas of responsibility include research, innovation and collaboration in the communications and IT sectors, and it publishes its general plan, policies, laws and regulations on its official website. MCIT is headquartered in Kabul. In late 2021, following the change of government, state telecommunications bodies including the Afghanistan Telecom Regulatory Authority (ATRA), the state-owned operator Afghan Telecom (Aftel), and Afghan Post were brought under the administrative umbrella of MCIT, with ATRA continuing to operate as a non-budgetary regulatory unit under the ministry's oversight. MCIT also lists online public services on its website, including a passport-tracking service and the e-Tazkera (electronic national ID) system.
retrieved_documents.source: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, official website

Answer: World Bank World Development Indicators estimate Afghanistan's total population at approximately 42,647,492 people in 2024, up from approximately 41,454,761 in 2023.

evidence.query: What was Afghanistan's total population in 2024, according to World Bank estimates?

retrieved_documents.title: Afghanistan Total Population, 2024
retrieved_documents.text: World Bank World Development Indicators estimate Afghanistan's total population at approximately 42,647,492 people in 2024, up from approximately 41,454,761 in 2023. The estimate uses a de facto definition of population, counting all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship, with the exception of refugees not permanently settled in Afghanistan. Afghanistan's annual population growth rate was estimated at approximately 2.8% in 2024. The population has a notably young age structure: World Bank data indicate that people aged 0-14 made up approximately 42.9% of the total population in 2024.

retrieved_documents.title: Urban Population Share in Afghanistan, 2024
retrieved_documents.text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, approximately 25.7% of Afghanistan's population lived in urban areas in 2024, up slightly from approximately 25.5% in 2023. Afghanistan remains one of the least-urbanized countries tracked by the World Bank, with the large majority of the population living in rural areas.

retrieved_documents.title: Median Age and Fertility Rate in Afghanistan
retrieved_documents.text: According to the UN Population Division's World Population Prospects (2024 revision), Afghanistan's median age is approximately 17.4 years, reflecting a very young population structure. Afghanistan's total fertility rate was approximately 4.84 births per woman in 2023, among the higher fertility rates outside of Africa, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data. This fertility rate has been on a long-term declining trend from higher levels in previous decades, but remains well above the global replacement-level rate of approximately 2.1 births per woman.
retrieved_documents.source: UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division (via Worldometer/Our World in Data)

retrieved_documents.text: According to data attributed to Afghanistan's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) and cited in an academic study of the sector, the total number of active users across Afghanistan's telecommunications market (combining mobile and internet services) reached 25.3 million in 2024. The same study notes a lack of market competition among network operators as a factor that keeps prices relatively high and reduces incentives to improve service quality.

retrieved_documents.title: Mes Aynak Copper Mine
retrieved_documents.text: Mes Aynak, located approximately 40 kilometres south-east of Kabul in Logar Province, is one of the world's largest known copper deposits. Estimates of the deposit's size vary significantly by source: a 2021 industry filing by the Metallurgical Corporation of China (MCC) put contained copper at approximately 11.08 million metric tons, while other press reports cite figures ranging from roughly 5.5 to over 12 million metric tons. In July 2024, representatives of Afghanistan's Taliban government and Chinese engineers held a groundbreaking ceremony for initial infrastructure (an access road) at the site, after a 30-year lease originally signed with MCC in 2008 had been delayed for approximately 16 years due to security and contractual issues.

retrieved_documents.title: Administrative Divisions of Afghanistan: Provinces and Districts
retrieved_documents.text: Afghanistan's administrative structure consists of 34 provinces (wilayat), which form the first-level administrative division of the country, and 401 districts (woleswali), which form the second-level division beneath the provinces. Provincial administrative boundaries are delineated by the Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), which is recognized as the country's authoritative source for administrative boundary delimitation. The AGCHO boundary dataset is distributed internationally through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) as part of the Common Operational Datasets (COD) used by the humanitarian community.
retrieved_documents.source: Common Operational Dataset - Administrative Boundaries (COD-AB), Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), distributed via UN OCHA / Humanitarian Data Exchange

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) is the government body responsible for telecommunications policy, internet-sector regulation and information-technology development in Afghanistan. Its published areas of responsibility include research, innovation and collaboration in the communications and IT sectors, and it publishes its general plan, policies, laws and regulations on its official website. MCIT is headquartered in Kabul. In late 2021, following the change of government, state telecommunications bodies including the Afghanistan Telecom Regulatory Authority (ATRA), the state-owned operator Afghan Telecom (Aftel), and Afghan Post were brought under the administrative umbrella of MCIT, with ATRA continuing to operate as a non-budgetary regulatory unit under the ministry's oversight. MCIT also lists online public services on its website, including a passport-tracking service and the e-Tazkera (electronic national ID) system.
retrieved_documents.source: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, official website

retrieved_documents.title: Afghanistan's Location, Borders, and Topography
retrieved_documents.text: Afghanistan is a landlocked country in south-central Asia with a total land boundary of approximately 5,987 km. It shares borders with six countries: Pakistan (2,670 km), Tajikistan (1,357 km), Turkmenistan (804 km), Iran (921 km), Uzbekistan (144 km), and China (91 km, via the narrow Wakhan Corridor in the country's far northeast). Afghanistan has no coastline and no maritime claims. The terrain is dominated by rugged mountains, including the Hindu Kush range, with plains in the north and southwest. The country's highest point is Noshak, at 7,492 metres above sea level, and its lowest point is along the Amu Darya river, at 258 metres above sea level.

retrieved_documents.title: Afghanistan's Lithium and Rare Earth Mineral Deposits
retrieved_documents.text: Afghanistan is reported to hold substantial lithium and rare-earth-element (REE) deposits, identified primarily in Ghazni, Nuristan, Helmand, Kunar, and Badakhshan provinces. Citing U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) estimates, press sources report Afghanistan's rare-earth deposits at approximately 1.4 million metric tons, alongside large iron-ore deposits (the Hajigak deposit; see DOC-048). As of the sources reviewed, these lithium and rare-earth deposits remain largely unexploited, without confirmed large-scale extraction contracts comparable to the Mes Aynak copper project.
retrieved_documents.source: Geopolitical Monitor; Eurasia Review (cross-checked, USGS-attributed estimates)

retrieved_documents.title: Population Density and Land Area of Afghanistan
retrieved_documents.text: Afghanistan's population density was approximately 63.8 people per square kilometre in 2023, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data, calculated against the country's total land area of approximately 652,860 square kilometres (see DOC-029). As of 2020 estimates cited by the same source, roughly 15.6% of Afghanistan's population lived in rural areas, 44.7% in towns, and 39.7% in cities under one classification scheme; this differs somewhat from the simpler urban/rural split reported by the World Bank in DOC-018, since different sources use different urban/rural/town classification methodologies.
retrieved_documents.source: Our World in Data; Worldometer (cross-checked, both citing UN Population Division)

Afghanistan is a landlocked country in south-central Asia with a total land boundary of approximately 5,987 km. It shares borders with six countries: Pakistan (2,670 km), Tajikistan (1,357 km), Turkmenistan (804 km), Iran (921 km), Uzbekistan (144 km), and China (91 km, via the narrow Wakhan Corridor in the country's far northeast). Afghanistan has no coastline and no maritime claims. The terrain is dominated by rugged mountains, including the Hindu Kush range, with plains in the north and southwest. The country's highest point is Noshak, at 7,492 metres above sea level, and its lowest point is along the Amu Darya river, at 258 metres above sea level.

Afghanistan's population density was approximately 63.8 people per square kilometre in 2023, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data, calculated against the country's total land area of approximately 652,860 square kilometres (see DOC-029). As of 2020 estimates cited by the same source, roughly 15.6% of Afghanistan's population lived in rural areas, 44.7% in towns, and 39.7% in cities under one classification scheme; this differs somewhat from the simpler urban/rural split reported by the World Bank in DOC-018, since different sources use different urban/rural/town classification methodologies.

According to World Bank World Development Indicators, which source their internet-usage figures from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), approximately 17.7% of Afghanistan's population were internet users in 2023, up from approximately 17.2% in 2022. 'Internet users' is defined as individuals who used the internet from any location, including via a computer or mobile phone, within the last three months. Internet penetration in Afghanistan has grown slowly and unevenly since 2001, rising from close to 0% in the early 2000s to the current level, and remains among the lowest of any country tracked by the World Bank.

retrieved_documents.title: Da Afghanistan Bank (Central Bank of Afghanistan)
retrieved_documents.text: Da Afghanistan Bank (DAB) is the central bank of Afghanistan, established in 1939 and wholly state-owned. It is responsible for formulating and implementing monetary policy, regulating and supervising financial institutions, managing currency issuance, and overseeing the national payment system. DAB is headquartered in Kabul. According to DAB's own published licensing information, Afghanistan's banking sector consists of 12 operational banks: 3 state-owned commercial banks, 7 private banks, and 2 branches of foreign banks. Individual customers are permitted to withdraw up to 350,000 Afghanis (approximately US$5,000) per week from their accounts.
retrieved_documents.source: Da Afghanistan Bank, official website; Wikipedia (cross-check)

retrieved_documents.title: Higher Education Institutions and Enrollment in Afghanistan
retrieved_documents.text: As of a 2017 World Bank feature report, Afghanistan had 36 public universities and institutes of higher education, most established or re-established within the preceding decade under the Higher Education Development Project (HEDP). A later report by Pajhwok Afghan News, published in August 2023, cited the Ministry of Higher Education's deputy minister stating that more than 400,000 students in total were studying across the country's universities, with approximately 180,000 enrolled in public universities specifically. In December 2022, the Taliban administration barred women from attending public and private universities, a policy that remained in effect as of the most recent reporting reviewed for this record; this materially affects how any pre-2022 and post-2022 enrollment figures should be compared.
retrieved_documents.source: World Bank (2017 feature article); Pajhwok Afghan News (2023 report)

retrieved_documents.title: Da Afghanistan Breshna Sherkat (DABS) - National Electricity Utility
retrieved_documents.text: Da Afghanistan Breshna Sherkat (DABS) is Afghanistan's national electricity utility, incorporated on 4 May 2008 (15 Saur 1387) as a limited-liability company wholly owned by the Government of Afghanistan, replacing the former Da Afghanistan Breshna Moassassa. DABS is responsible for electricity generation, import, transmission, and distribution nationwide on a commercial basis. Afghanistan remains substantially dependent on imported electricity from neighboring countries, including Iran, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, and Tajikistan, particularly during winter months and periods of peak demand, since domestic generation capacity covers only a fraction of national demand.
retrieved_documents.source: Da Afghanistan Breshna Sherkat, official website; Devex organization profile (cross-check)

retrieved_documents.title: Afghan Telecom and the National Fiber-Optic Backbone
retrieved_documents.text: Afghan Telecom (branded 'Salaam' for retail mobile service) is a government-owned telecommunications company established in 2006, tasked with operating government telecommunications networks, including Afghanistan's fiber-optic backbone. Afghan Telecom operates as part of the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT, see DOC-003). As a state-owned operator with a universal-service mandate, it has historically had a smaller subscriber share than the country's private mobile operators.
retrieved_documents.source: Academic study of Afghanistan's telecommunications sector

Afghanistan's trade balance has been negative for an extended period, reflecting the country's reliance on imported goods relative to its export base, which is concentrated in agricultural products such as dried fruits and nuts.

Answer: Through its Civil Registration and Foreign Nationals Registration Department, NSIA is also responsible for registering Afghan citizens and issuing documents including national ID cards (e-Tazkera), birth certificates, death certificates, and marriage certificates.

evidence.query: Which Afghan government body is responsible for civil registration and issuing national ID cards (e-Tazkera)?

retrieved_documents.title: National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA) and the e-Tazkera System
retrieved_documents.text: The National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA), formerly known as the Central Statistics Office, is the Afghan government agency responsible for collecting and maintaining the country's statistical data. It was established in 1972. Through its Civil Registration and Foreign Nationals Registration Department, NSIA is also responsible for registering Afghan citizens and issuing documents including national ID cards (e-Tazkera), birth certificates, death certificates, and marriage certificates. According to a July 2025 report by Pajhwok Afghan News, NSIA officials stated that more than 16 million electronic ID cards had been distributed countrywide to date, of which approximately 10 million were issued after the change of government in 2021.
retrieved_documents.source: National Statistics and Information Authority, official website; Pajhwok Afghan News

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Energy and Water
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Energy and Water is the Afghan government body responsible for national energy policy and water-resource management, including hydropower development, irrigation infrastructure, and water-basin management. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1980. It is headquartered in Kabul.
retrieved_documents.source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Economy
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Economy is responsible for macroeconomic planning, coordinating development programs, and compiling national economic statistics in cooperation with other government bodies such as the National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA, see DOC-020). According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1920.
retrieved_documents.source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) is the government body responsible for telecommunications policy, internet-sector regulation and information-technology development in Afghanistan. Its published areas of responsibility include research, innovation and collaboration in the communications and IT sectors, and it publishes its general plan, policies, laws and regulations on its official website. MCIT is headquartered in Kabul. In late 2021, following the change of government, state telecommunications bodies including the Afghanistan Telecom Regulatory Authority (ATRA), the state-owned operator Afghan Telecom (Aftel), and Afghan Post were brought under the administrative umbrella of MCIT, with ATRA continuing to operate as a non-budgetary regulatory unit under the ministry's oversight. MCIT also lists online public services on its website, including a passport-tracking service and the e-Tazkera (electronic national ID) system.
retrieved_documents.source: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, official website

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Higher Education (MoHE)
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Higher Education (MoHE) is the Afghan government body responsible for regulating, expanding, and developing the country's institutions of higher education. Its responsibilities include developing a national higher-education curriculum, teacher training, in-service training for university faculty, partnerships with international universities, and providing training in accounting, management, and computer literacy for university administration. A separate Ministry of Higher Education was first proposed in 1973 and was formally established in 1977, standardizing what had previously been managed through the Ministry of Education.
retrieved_documents.source: Ministry of Higher Education, official website; academic secondary source (cross-check for founding date)

Answer: Kandahar is the capital of Kandahar Province in southern Afghanistan and served as the first capital of the Durrani Empire before the seat of government moved to Kabul in 1776.

evidence.query: Kandahar is the capital of which Afghan province?

retrieved_documents.title: Herat, Kandahar, and Mazar-i-Sharif: Major Provincial Capitals
retrieved_documents.text: Herat is the capital of Herat Province in western Afghanistan, situated in the valley of the Hari River near the borders with Iran and Turkmenistan; it is one of the country's oldest cities and a historic center on the Silk Road. Kandahar is the capital of Kandahar Province in southern Afghanistan and served as the first capital of the Durrani Empire before the seat of government moved to Kabul in 1776. Mazar-i-Sharif is the capital of Balkh Province in northern Afghanistan, close to the borders with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and is home to the Shrine of Ali (the 'Blue Mosque'), one of the country's most-visited religious sites.
retrieved_documents.source: General geographic reference, cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset

retrieved_documents.title: Founding of Modern Afghanistan
retrieved_documents.text: The modern state of Afghanistan traces its founding to 1747, when Ahmad Shah Durrani unified the Pashtun tribes and established the Durrani Empire, initially with its capital at Kandahar; the capital was later moved to Kabul in 1776. Afghanistan served as a buffer state between the British and Russian empires through the 19th century, a period often referred to as 'The Great Game.' It won full independence over its foreign affairs from British control in 1919, following the Third Anglo-Afghan War.

retrieved_documents.title: Southern and South-Eastern Afghanistan: Provinces and Capitals
retrieved_documents.text: Southern and south-eastern Afghanistan border Pakistan and include some of the country's largest provinces by land area. Helmand Province, the largest Afghan province by area, has its capital at Lashkargah. Zabul Province's capital is Qalat (also called Qalat-i Ghilji). Uruzgan Province's capital is Tarinkot. Khost Province's capital is Khost city. Paktia Province's capital is Gardez. Paktika Province's capital is Sharana. Nimroz Province, in the country's south-west, has its capital at Zaranj, near the border with Iran.
retrieved_documents.source: General geographic reference (Wikipedia province/capital listings), cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset

retrieved_documents.title: Kabul: National Capital and Capital of Kabul Province
retrieved_documents.text: Kabul is the national capital of Afghanistan and simultaneously serves as the capital of Kabul Province, one of Afghanistan's 34 provinces. Kabul Province is located in the eastern-central part of the country and borders Parwan, Kapisa, Laghman, Nangarhar, Logar and Maidan Wardak provinces. As the seat of the national government, Kabul city hosts the country's central government ministries and foreign diplomatic missions, and it is the largest urban center among all Afghan provinces. The dual role of Kabul as both national capital and provincial capital is consistent across administrative-boundary datasets maintained by AGCHO and distributed through UN OCHA's Common Operational Datasets programme.

Answer: The Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) is the Afghan government body tasked with delivering and promoting sustainable, accessible health care services nationwide.

evidence.query: Which ministry is responsible for public health services in Afghanistan?

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Public Health (MoPH)
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) is the Afghan government body tasked with delivering and promoting sustainable, accessible health care services nationwide. Its published mandate covers health-service delivery, health-system policy and planning, and administration and finance for the health sector. MoPH is organized into directorates for policy and planning and for health-service provision, alongside programs such as a national cancer-control program and hospital-reform initiatives. MoPH publishes news, laws, regulations, strategies, and reports on its official website.
retrieved_documents.source: Ministry of Public Health, official website

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Public Works
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Public Works is responsible for the construction and maintenance of Afghanistan's national highway network and other major public infrastructure projects. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1933.
retrieved_documents.source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock (MAIL) is responsible for agricultural policy, irrigation systems, and livestock and veterinary services in Afghanistan, an economy in which agriculture remains one of the largest employment sectors. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, MAIL was founded in 1918, making it one of the country's oldest government ministries.
retrieved_documents.source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website

retrieved_documents.title: Higher Education Institutions and Enrollment in Afghanistan
retrieved_documents.text: As of a 2017 World Bank feature report, Afghanistan had 36 public universities and institutes of higher education, most established or re-established within the preceding decade under the Higher Education Development Project (HEDP). A later report by Pajhwok Afghan News, published in August 2023, cited the Ministry of Higher Education's deputy minister stating that more than 400,000 students in total were studying across the country's universities, with approximately 180,000 enrolled in public universities specifically. In December 2022, the Taliban administration barred women from attending public and private universities, a policy that remained in effect as of the most recent reporting reviewed for this record; this materially affects how any pre-2022 and post-2022 enrollment figures should be compared.
retrieved_documents.source: World Bank (2017 feature article); Pajhwok Afghan News (2023 report)

retrieved_documents.title: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
retrieved_documents.text: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) is the government body responsible for telecommunications policy, internet-sector regulation and information-technology development in Afghanistan. Its published areas of responsibility include research, innovation and collaboration in the communications and IT sectors, and it publishes its general plan, policies, laws and regulations on its official website. MCIT is headquartered in Kabul. In late 2021, following the change of government, state telecommunications bodies including the Afghanistan Telecom Regulatory Authority (ATRA), the state-owned operator Afghan Telecom (Aftel), and Afghan Post were brought under the administrative umbrella of MCIT, with ATRA continuing to operate as a non-budgetary regulatory unit under the ministry's oversight. MCIT also lists online public services on its website, including a passport-tracking service and the e-Tazkera (electronic national ID) system.
retrieved_documents.source: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, official website

Its published mandate covers health-service delivery, health-system policy and planning, and administration and finance for the health sector. MoPH is organized into directorates for policy and planning and for health-service provision, alongside programs such as a national cancer-control program and hospital-reform initiatives. MoPH publishes news, laws, regulations, strategies, and reports on its official website.

The Ministry of Public Works is responsible for the construction and maintenance of Afghanistan's national highway network and other major public infrastructure projects. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1933.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock (MAIL) is responsible for agricultural policy, irrigation systems, and livestock and veterinary services in Afghanistan, an economy in which agriculture remains one of the largest employment sectors. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, MAIL was founded in 1918, making it one of the country's oldest government ministries.

As of a 2017 World Bank feature report, Afghanistan had 36 public universities and institutes of higher education, most established or re-established within the preceding decade under the Higher Education Development Project (HEDP). A later report by Pajhwok Afghan News, published in August 2023, cited the Ministry of Higher Education's deputy minister stating that more than 400,000 students in total were studying across the country's universities, with approximately 180,000 enrolled in public universities specifically. In December 2022, the Taliban administration barred women from attending public and private universities, a policy that remained in effect as of the most recent reporting reviewed for this record; this materially affects how any pre-2022 and post-2022 enrollment figures should be compared.

The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) is the government body responsible for telecommunications policy, internet-sector regulation and information-technology development in Afghanistan. Its published areas of responsibility include research, innovation and collaboration in the communications and IT sectors, and it publishes its general plan, policies, laws and regulations on its official website. MCIT is headquartered in Kabul. In late 2021, following the change of government, state telecommunications bodies including the Afghanistan Telecom Regulatory Authority (ATRA), the state-owned operator Afghan Telecom (Aftel), and Afghan Post were brought under the administrative umbrella of MCIT, with ATRA continuing to operate as a non-budgetary regulatory unit under the ministry's oversight. MCIT also lists online public services on its website, including a passport-tracking service and the e-Tazkera (electronic national ID) system.

Answer: Afghanistan's official currency is the Afghani, with the ISO 4217 currency code AFN.

evidence.query: What is the ISO 4217 currency code for the Afghan afghani?

retrieved_documents.title: The Afghan Afghani (AFN)
retrieved_documents.text: Afghanistan's official currency is the Afghani, with the ISO 4217 currency code AFN. The Afghani is issued exclusively by Da Afghanistan Bank (DAB), the country's central bank, which is also responsible for printing Afghani banknotes as part of its function as the state's currency-issuing authority. DAB regulations permit individual bank customers to withdraw up to 350,000 Afghanis (roughly US$5,000) per week, or up to 1,000,000 Afghanis per month, from their bank accounts.

retrieved_documents.title: Afghanistan Gross Domestic Product (GDP), 2023
retrieved_documents.text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators data, Afghanistan's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at current prices was approximately US$17.15 billion in 2023, up from approximately US$14.50 billion in 2022. GDP is measured as the sum of gross value added by all resident producers in the economy, plus product taxes and minus subsidies, without deductions for depreciation of assets. Dollar figures are converted from Afghanistan's domestic currency (the Afghani) using official exchange rates for the corresponding year. The services sector is the largest contributor to Afghanistan's GDP, followed by agriculture. World Bank data put GDP per capita for the same year at approximately US$378.

retrieved_documents.title: Da Afghanistan Bank (Central Bank of Afghanistan)
retrieved_documents.text: Da Afghanistan Bank (DAB) is the central bank of Afghanistan, established in 1939 and wholly state-owned. It is responsible for formulating and implementing monetary policy, regulating and supervising financial institutions, managing currency issuance, and overseeing the national payment system. DAB is headquartered in Kabul. According to DAB's own published licensing information, Afghanistan's banking sector consists of 12 operational banks: 3 state-owned commercial banks, 7 private banks, and 2 branches of foreign banks. Individual customers are permitted to withdraw up to 350,000 Afghanis (approximately US$5,000) per week from their accounts.
retrieved_documents.source: Da Afghanistan Bank, official website; Wikipedia (cross-check)

Answer: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, approximately 25.7% of Afghanistan's population lived in urban areas in 2024, up slightly from approximately 25.5% in 2023.

evidence.query: What percentage of Afghanistan's population was urban in 2024, according to the World Bank?

retrieved_documents.title: Urban Population Share in Afghanistan, 2024
retrieved_documents.text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, approximately 25.7% of Afghanistan's population lived in urban areas in 2024, up slightly from approximately 25.5% in 2023. Afghanistan remains one of the least-urbanized countries tracked by the World Bank, with the large majority of the population living in rural areas.

retrieved_documents.title: Afghanistan Total Population, 2024
retrieved_documents.text: World Bank World Development Indicators estimate Afghanistan's total population at approximately 42,647,492 people in 2024, up from approximately 41,454,761 in 2023. The estimate uses a de facto definition of population, counting all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship, with the exception of refugees not permanently settled in Afghanistan. Afghanistan's annual population growth rate was estimated at approximately 2.8% in 2024. The population has a notably young age structure: World Bank data indicate that people aged 0-14 made up approximately 42.9% of the total population in 2024.

retrieved_documents.title: Median Age and Fertility Rate in Afghanistan
retrieved_documents.text: According to the UN Population Division's World Population Prospects (2024 revision), Afghanistan's median age is approximately 17.4 years, reflecting a very young population structure. Afghanistan's total fertility rate was approximately 4.84 births per woman in 2023, among the higher fertility rates outside of Africa, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data. This fertility rate has been on a long-term declining trend from higher levels in previous decades, but remains well above the global replacement-level rate of approximately 2.1 births per woman.
retrieved_documents.source: UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division (via Worldometer/Our World in Data)

retrieved_documents.title: Mes Aynak Copper Mine
retrieved_documents.text: Mes Aynak, located approximately 40 kilometres south-east of Kabul in Logar Province, is one of the world's largest known copper deposits. Estimates of the deposit's size vary significantly by source: a 2021 industry filing by the Metallurgical Corporation of China (MCC) put contained copper at approximately 11.08 million metric tons, while other press reports cite figures ranging from roughly 5.5 to over 12 million metric tons. In July 2024, representatives of Afghanistan's Taliban government and Chinese engineers held a groundbreaking ceremony for initial infrastructure (an access road) at the site, after a 30-year lease originally signed with MCC in 2008 had been delayed for approximately 16 years due to security and contractual issues.
retrieved_documents.source: The Diplomat; RFE/RL Radio Azadi; USGS Minerals Yearbook (cross-checked)

retrieved_documents.text: According to data attributed to Afghanistan's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) and cited in an academic study of the sector, the total number of active users across Afghanistan's telecommunications market (combining mobile and internet services) reached 25.3 million in 2024. The same study notes a lack of market competition among network operators as a factor that keeps prices relatively high and reduces incentives to improve service quality.

evidence.context:
According to World Bank World Development Indicators, approximately 25.7% of Afghanistan's population lived in urban areas in 2024, up slightly from approximately 25.5% in 2023. Afghanistan remains one of the least-urbanized countries tracked by the World Bank, with the large majority of the population living in rural areas.

World Bank World Development Indicators estimate Afghanistan's total population at approximately 42,647,492 people in 2024, up from approximately 41,454,761 in 2023. The estimate uses a de facto definition of population, counting all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship, with the exception of refugees not permanently settled in Afghanistan. Afghanistan's annual population growth rate was estimated at approximately 2.8% in 2024. The population has a notably young age structure: World Bank data indicate that people aged 0-14 made up approximately 42.9% of the total population in 2024.

According to the UN Population Division's World Population Prospects (2024 revision), Afghanistan's median age is approximately 17.4 years, reflecting a very young population structure. Afghanistan's total fertility rate was approximately 4.84 births per woman in 2023, among the higher fertility rates outside of Africa, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data. This fertility rate has been on a long-term declining trend from higher levels in previous decades, but remains well above the global replacement-level rate of approximately 2.1 births per woman.

Mes Aynak, located approximately 40 kilometres south-east of Kabul in Logar Province, is one of the world's largest known copper deposits. Estimates of the deposit's size vary significantly by source: a 2021 industry filing by the Metallurgical Corporation of China (MCC) put contained copper at approximately 11.08 million metric tons, while other press reports cite figures ranging from roughly 5.5 to over 12 million metric tons. In July 2024, representatives of Afghanistan's Taliban government and Chinese engineers held a groundbreaking ceremony for initial infrastructure (an access road) at the site, after a 30-year lease originally signed with MCC in 2008 had been delayed for approximately 16 years due to security and contractual issues.

retrieved_documents.title: Population Density and Land Area of Afghanistan
retrieved_documents.text: Afghanistan's population density was approximately 63.8 people per square kilometre in 2023, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data, calculated against the country's total land area of approximately 652,860 square kilometres (see DOC-029). As of 2020 estimates cited by the same source, roughly 15.6% of Afghanistan's population lived in rural areas, 44.7% in towns, and 39.7% in cities under one classification scheme; this differs somewhat from the simpler urban/rural split reported by the World Bank in DOC-018, since different sources use different urban/rural/town classification methodologies.

Afghanistan's population density was approximately 63.8 people per square kilometre in 2023, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data, calculated against the country's total land area of approximately 652,860 square kilometres (see DOC-029). As of 2020 estimates cited by the same source, roughly 15.6% of Afghanistan's population lived in rural areas, 44.7% in towns, and 39.7% in cities under one classification scheme; this differs somewhat from the simpler urban/rural split reported by the World Bank in DOC-018, since different sources use different urban/rural/town classification methodologies.

retrieved_documents.title: Adult Literacy Rate in Afghanistan, 2021

retrieved_documents.title: Population Density and Land Area of Afghanistan
retrieved_documents.text: Afghanistan's population density was approximately 63.8 people per square kilometre in 2023, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data, calculated against the country's total land area of approximately 652,860 square kilometres (see DOC-029). retrieved_documents.title: Afghanistan Total Population, 2024
retrieved_documents.text: World Bank World Development Indicators estimate Afghanistan's total population at approximately 42,647,492 people in 2024, up from approximately 41,454,761 in 2023. The population has a notably young age structure: World Bank data indicate that people aged 0-14 made up approximately 42.9% of the total population in 2024.

World Bank World Development Indicators estimate Afghanistan's total population at approximately 42,647,492 people in 2024, up from approximately 41,454,761 in 2023. The estimate uses a de facto definition of population, counting all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship, with the exception of refugees not permanently settled in Afghanistan. Afghanistan's annual population growth rate was estimated at approximately 2.8% in 2024. The population has a notably young age structure: World Bank data indicate that people aged 0-14 made up approximately 42.9% of the total population in 2024.

retrieved_documents.title: Administrative Divisions of Afghanistan: Provinces and Districts
retrieved_documents.text: The AGCHO boundary dataset is distributed internationally through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) as part of the Common Operational Datasets (COD) used by the humanitarian community. The current 34-province, 401-district structure was established in the boundary dataset released on 22 October 2019 and was most recently reviewed for accuracy in July 2024, with reviewers determining that no update to the boundaries was required at that time. Each province is subdivided into a number of districts, ranging from as few as 6 districts (Nimroz) to as many as 28 districts (Badakhshan) in the AGCHO dataset. Provinces are governed by a provincial governor, and districts are the primary unit for local public-service delivery, including health, education and security administration.

The current 34-province, 401-district structure was established in the boundary dataset released on 22 October 2019 and was most recently reviewed for accuracy in July 2024, with reviewers determining that no update to the boundaries was required at that time. Each province is subdivided into a number of districts, ranging from as few as 6 districts (Nimroz) to as many as 28 districts (Badakhshan) in the AGCHO dataset. retrieved_documents.title: Administrative Divisions of Afghanistan: Provinces and Districts
retrieved_documents.text: The AGCHO boundary dataset is distributed internationally through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) as part of the Common Operational Datasets (COD) used by the humanitarian community. The current 34-province, 401-district structure was established in the boundary dataset released on 22 October 2019 and was most recently reviewed for accuracy in July 2024, with reviewers determining that no update to the boundaries was required at that time. Each province is subdivided into a number of districts, ranging from as few as 6 districts (Nimroz) to as many as 28 districts (Badakhshan) in the AGCHO dataset. Provinces are governed by a provincial governor, and districts are the primary unit for local public-service delivery, including health, education and security administration.

retrieved_documents.title: Recent Changes in Girls' Primary School Enrollment
retrieved_documents.text: According to UNESCO data reported by UN News, Afghanistan had approximately 5.7 million girls and boys enrolled in primary school in 2022, down from approximately 6.8 million in 2019. UN News attributes this decline in part to the Taliban administration's restrictions on female teachers instructing male students, which has worsened an existing teacher shortage, alongside broader socioeconomic pressures on families. Girls' enrollment in primary education (technically still permitted under the Taliban administration for girls under approximately 12 years old) has fallen since 2021, distinct from the separate restriction on women's access to secondary and university education (see DOC-019).

retrieved_documents.title: Internet Usage in Afghanistan, 2023
retrieved_documents.text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, which source their internet-usage figures from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), approximately 17.7% of Afghanistan's population were internet users in 2023, up from approximately 17.2% in 2022. 'Internet users' is defined as individuals who used the internet from any location, including via a computer or mobile phone, within the last three months. Internet penetration in Afghanistan has grown slowly and unevenly since 2001, rising from close to 0% in the early 2000s to the current level, and remains among the lowest of any country tracked by the World Bank.
retrieved_documents.source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (sourced from the International Telecommunication Union)
